summary: Describes a format for an LDAP Uniform Resource Locator, allowing Internet clients direct access to the LDAP directory protocol. It is on the standards track as a proposed standard. It was replaced by RFC 2255.

eli5.summary: A web-style link that points straight into a directory of people and things, so programs can click and look them up.

questions: how to write an ldap url
subtitle: Web-style links to query LDAP directory servers.

tldr.problem: LDAP is a protocol for querying directory servers, but there was no standard way to express an LDAP query as a clickable URL, limiting how easily web browsers and applications could access directories.
tldr.mechanism: The LDAP URL format (ldap://hostname/distinguished-name?attributes?scope?filter) encodes the server, the directory entry path, which attributes to return, the search scope, and filter criteria in a single URL string, following RFC 1738 URL syntax.
tldr.outcome: Applications can now link directly to directory lookups, with support across various platforms. The format was later refined in RFC 2255.

today: RFC 1959 defined the LDAP URL format as a standards-track proposal. It was later refined and clarified in RFC 2255.

sections.title: URLs for Directory Lookups
sections.content:
LDAP is the Lightweight Directory Access Protocol, used to query directory servers like X.500 directories, address books, and people registries. Unlike HTTP, which has URLs (http://...) that web browsers understand and can link to, LDAP had no standard URL format. This RFC defines a syntax that lets LDAP queries be expressed as URLs, enabling web clients and applications to link directly to directory lookups.

The LDAP URL format is similar to HTTP URLs but specifies not just a server address but also what to search for and how.
sections.eli5: LDAP is like a big phone book that is searchable. A URL format lets you make a link that says "look up this person with these rules."

sections.title: LDAP URL Syntax and Parts
sections.content:
An LDAP URL begins with ldap:// and includes: an optional hostname and port (default port 389); a Distinguished Name (DN) path, which identifies the entry or subtree to search (required); zero to four optional query parts separated by ?: attributes (which attributes to return), scope (base, one, or sub), and filter (search criteria).

Example: ldap://ldap.example.com/o=Company,c=US?cn,mail?sub?(cn=John*) searches for all people whose name starts with "John", in the Company directory, returning their common name and email. If hostname is omitted, any X.500-capable LDAP server can resolve the query. URL-illegal characters like spaces are percent-encoded using the method from RFC 1738.
sections.eli5: The URL has the server address, the person or group you want (the path), and filters like "people whose name starts with Jo."

sections.title: Defaults and Search Behavior
sections.content:
If the attributes part is omitted, all attributes are returned. If scope is omitted, a base object search is assumed (only the entry itself, not its children). If filter is omitted, (objectClass=*) is assumed (match any object). When the hostname is missing and the DN is in the X.500 namespace, the URL can be resolved by any X.500-back-ended LDAP server.

Applications supporting LDAP URLs can click them like web links, construct them dynamically, or use them in configuration. However, the URL format does not provide a way to specify username and password, so LDAP URL queries are always unauthenticated.
sections.eli5: The URL has sensible defaults: if you do not specify what to search for, it finds anything. If you do not name a server, any directory server can answer.
